reference.source: ISSVA classification / Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies
clinicalPearls: An aggressive complex lymphatic anomaly distinguished from generalised lymphatic anomaly by clusters of spindled lymphatic endothelial cells and a marked bleeding tendency
It characteristically causes haemorrhagic pleural and pericardial effusions and a consumptive coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia and hypofibrinogenaemia
Thoracic and mediastinal involvement is common and drives respiratory morbidity and mortality
Somatic activating NRAS variants have been identified, placing it within the RAS-pathway lymphatic anomalies
Histology shows dilated lymphatic channels accompanied by characteristic foci of spindled lymphatic endothelial cells, unlike generalised lymphatic anomaly
The coagulopathy resembles but is mechanistically distinct from the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon of vascular tumours
Sirolimus, sometimes combined with MEK-pathway inhibition in refractory disease, is used for medical control alongside supportive management
It carries the worst prognosis among the complex lymphatic anomalies and needs specialist multidisciplinary care
reference.pathophysiology: Kaposiform lymphangiomatosis is an aggressive, multifocal lymphatic malformation in which abnormal, dilated lymphatic channels are interspersed with clusters and sheets of spindled lymphatic endothelial cells. Somatic activating variants in NRAS drive dysregulated RAS-MAPK signalling within the lymphatic endothelium. The disordered lymphatics and abnormal endothelium promote platelet activation and consumption of clotting factors, producing thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenaemia and a bleeding diathesis that manifests as haemorrhagic effusions. Extensive thoracic involvement leads to progressive respiratory compromise.
additionalDifferentials: Generalised lymphatic anomaly (no spindle cells, milder coagulopathy)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and coagulation profile including fibrinogen and D-dimer to document consumptive coagulopathy
MRI and CT of the chest to map mediastinal and pulmonary involvement
Analysis of pleural or pericardial fluid, often haemorrhagic
Biopsy showing spindled lymphatic endothelial cells with lymphatic markers
Molecular testing for NRAS and related RAS-pathway variants
redFlags: Haemorrhagic pleural or pericardial effusions with respiratory or cardiac compromise
Severe thrombocytopenia and hypofibrinogenaemia with bleeding
Refractory chylous or bloody effusions despite drainage
reference.prognosis: Kaposiform lymphangiomatosis has the most guarded prognosis of the complex lymphatic anomalies, with significant mortality from haemorrhage and respiratory failure; sirolimus and RAS/MEK-directed therapy have improved outcomes but the disease is chronic and often difficult to control.
pitfalls: Mislabelling it as generalised lymphatic anomaly and underestimating the bleeding and effusion risk
Overlooking the consumptive coagulopathy before drainage or surgery
Assuming effusions are infective or malignant rather than haemorrhagic-lymphatic
Delaying systemic therapy in favour of repeated procedural drainage alone
references: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Haemangiomas and Malformations
management: Use sirolimus as the mainstay systemic therapy, with RAS/MEK-directed agents such as trametinib given the activating NRAS pathway
Support the consumptive coagulopathy with fibrinogen and clotting-factor replacement and cautious blood-product use
Drain and manage haemorrhagic pleural and pericardial effusions with respiratory support
Monitor platelets, fibrinogen and D-dimer serially and map thoracic disease with cross-sectional imaging
Undertake molecular testing for NRAS and related RAS-pathway variants to guide targeted therapy
Manage within a multidisciplinary vascular anomalies team given the guarded, chronic course
